analysis.one_liner: Requires the White House to report to Congress before negotiating any deal that would weaken U.S. patent or copyright rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced on November 8, 2024, it was sent to two House committees and sat there until the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the President and U.S. trade negotiators to file a report with Congress at least 60 days before starting any negotiation that could weaken American patent, copyright, trademark, trade secret, or plant variety rights. The report would have to analyze how the possible outcomes would affect rights-holders — a category the bill defines to explicitly include U.S. corporations. It never moved past its initial committee referrals.
analysis.who_benefits: Holders of U.S. intellectual property rights would gain: before any U.S. negotiation that could reduce the value, scope, or enforceability of a patent, copyright, trademark, trade secret, or plant variety right, the administration would have to give the House and Senate Judiciary Committees an advance impact analysis [S2]. The protected rights-holders, defined as "United States persons," expressly include corporations and partnerships organized under U.S. law [S2]. In practice the bill is aimed at waiver negotiations — the short title is the "Timely Reporting of IP Rights Waivers Act" [S2] — such as the WTO TRIPS waivers countries seek so generic versions of patented medicines can be made during emergencies. Pharmaceutical companies and other patent-heavy industries would gain a new procedural roadblock against agreements that thin out their rights.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patent and copyright holders, including corporations

how_it_helps.text: The bill obligates the President or any U.S. negotiator to submit a report to both Judiciary Committees, at least 60 days before negotiations begin, analyzing how any deal that would reduce or restrict patent, copyright, trademark, trade secret, or plant variety rights would affect those rights and their holders.

The rights-holders whose interests must be analyzed, "United States persons," expressly include corporations, partnerships, and other organizations organized under U.S. law — so the mandated analysis is centered on business interests rather than consumers.

The bill's short title, the "Timely Reporting of IP Rights Waivers Act," signals its purpose: inserting an advance-notice and analysis step before any negotiation over waiving intellectual property obligations, the mechanism used in WTO TRIPS waivers that open the door to generic versions of patented drugs.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and patients would bear the indirect cost if the bill passed: negotiations that could expand access to affordable generic medicines or otherwise ease patent and copyright restrictions would face a mandatory 60-day delay and a one-sided analysis focused on rights-holders, making such deals slower and harder to conclude. The executive branch would also bear the burden of preparing the reports.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers, especially patients waiting on generics

drawbacks.text: The required analysis counts only losses to rights-holders; the bill demands no assessment of what consumers or patients would gain from a negotiated change, such as lower generic drug prices — so the reporting is built to weigh one side's interests and none of the public's.

A 60-day advance reporting requirement would delay and could deter executive-branch negotiators from pursuing international agreements that reduce intellectual property restrictions, including ones meant to expand access to medicines abroad.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's practical effect is small on its face — reports, not bans — but its design is one-sided: it creates friction for exactly the negotiations that could lower medicine prices and ease IP restrictions, while requiring analysis only of harms to rights-holders, with no counterweight measuring consumer gains. Even supporters of strong intellectual property protection would have to acknowledge the bill functions as a procedural brake on waiver negotiations rather than as a transparency measure for the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Agriculture Committees the day it was introduced and never moved again — no hearing, no vote, nothing — and the Congress ended without it going anywhere.

narrative.text: Representative Darrell Issa introduced the bill on November 8, 2024, with Representative Scott Fitzgerald as an original cosponsor.
The same day, the House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and, for relevant provisions, to the Agriculture Committee.
No further action of any kind was taken; the bill was still sitting in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and all pending legislation died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed. The existing legal framework — which strongly protects patent, copyright, and trademark holders, including drug companies — stayed intact, and no new reporting hurdle was added for future waiver negotiations. Because no such negotiations were pending, no side gained anything concrete, though the status quo already favors intellectual-property-heavy industries.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the status quo held

for.name: Rep. Scott Fitzgerald
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; the bill drew only Republican cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after its November 2024 referral — no markup, no vote — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no voting pattern exists; the bill's only support on the record came from Republican sponsors, and no group or member is on record against it.

industries.industry: Pharmaceutical manufacturers and other patent-heavy industries
industries.note: The bill would give patent holders, including corporations, an advance impact analysis and congressional notice before any U.S. negotiation that could weaken patent rights — raising the cost of TRIPS-style waivers that enable generic competition with patented drugs. Patients and consumers, who benefit when patents ease, would face the added friction instead.

The same 60-day reporting requirement would attach to any negotiation touching copyright, protecting content industries from international agreements that loosen their rights. The public's direct stake here is smaller than with drug patents, though access and fair-use questions can arise in such deals.

Plant variety rights are explicitly covered, and the bill was also referred to the Agriculture Committee for those provisions — shielding breeders' rights from negotiated changes. The Agriculture referral is the clearest sign the bill's drafters saw farm-sector intellectual property as part of its scope.

By making it procedurally harder for the U.S. to negotiate waivers that reduce patent scope, the bill would narrow the openings through which generic manufacturers gain access to patented markets. That runs alongside patients' interest in lower prices.
